item.title: Self-Care for Burnout: Time Management and Micro Self-Care
item.description:
Maybe you’re among the millions of people who live an extraordinarily busy life. Juggling professional responsibilities as well as family and household activities can be extremely stressful. Unfortunately, self-care for burnout often takes a backseat to other seemingly more urgent activities.

Prioritizing Self-Care

You likely know that you should be prioritizing your health through self-care, but there are times in life when, for practical reasons, self-care falls down the list of priorities.

While this isn’t a sustainable lifestyle, there are times when neglecting self-care feels unavoidable in the short term. In those times, it’s likely you will feel the struggle. It might manifest itself as fatigue, stress, and feelings of being overwhelmed or burnout. Burnout is a state of emotional and physical depletion, not just a state of busyness resulting from a full calendar.

You might not have the budget for a full day at the spa, or even the time for an evening of DIY self-care, but everyone has a few moments in their day that can be allocated to self-care.

Recapture Time

Unless you are a genuinely fanatically organized person, you likely have moments in your day that could be better spent. A Texas A&M Transportation Institute’s 2025 Urban Mobility Report showed that Americans sat in traffic for sixty-three hours a year on average. That’s the highest level recorded since traffic tracking started in 1982.

Other studies have shown that Americans spend about three months’ worth of time per year waiting in various lines and over forty days on hold with customer service over the course of a lifetime. That’s a lot of hours wasted each year doing mundane and unavoidable things.

You can reclaim some of that time. Not only will this reduce stress, but it will free up time for self-care. But reclaiming your time only works if you protect that which has been reclaimed. If you save an hour by being efficient, it’s important to resist the urge to fill it with more chores.

Where Can I Find This Wasted Time?

Take a look at your daily life and search for wasted pockets of time. It may not seem worth the effort to recapture a minute here or five there, but if you learn how to maximize your reclaimed time, even if it seems minuscule, it can make a significant difference in your life.

To find these wasted moments, keep a journal. It may seem counterintuitive to add journaling to your already overpacked schedule, but if you commit to keeping track of your day, even in the short term, you’ll likely find many moments that you can optimize.

If you don’t have time to journal, simply check in with yourself periodically. Set a timer for three random points in your day and jot down one word describing what you’re doing and how you feel. You’ll quickly see a pattern of where your energy is being drained unnecessarily.

Implement micro self-care

Even the busiest people in the world have time for brief moments of self-care. Here are some ways that you can fit small moments of self-care into your day.

Use your commute

Use your commute time to catch up with old friends on a phone call (hands-free, of course). Download your favorite audiobook or simply relax with some of your favorite low-key music. If you want to maximize your time for work so that you can relax later, you might ask your boss if you can work remotely or change your hours so you don’t have to travel during peak rush hours.

If your job requires you to be physically present at specific times, focus instead on the sensory environment of your commute. Use a specific scent in your car or a particular playlist that signals to your brain that work is over and that it’s time to reset.

Make grocery shopping work for you

A lot of time is consumed by running errands like buying groceries. One way to mitigate wasted time is to use grocery delivery services. You will still get your favorite necessities, but instead of wasting time traveling to and from the grocery store, you can simply shop from the convenience of your home or office.

While it may feel like a financial luxury, you must also consider that your time is worth money. You may even be surprised at how much more productive you’ll be when you don’t have to worry about errands.

If delivery fees aren’t in the budget and you must do the grocery shopping yourself, try minimizing your need to make decisions. Stick to a standardized list of five rotating meals to eliminate the mental exhaustion of trying to figure out what’s for dinner.

You can also invite a friend along to do their shopping. That way, you can socialize while you’re doing your errands. Or find a few friends who are also busy and take turns doing each other’s shopping. Instead of going to the grocery store once a week, you can go once a month.

Digital time adds up

While traffic and grocery lines are unavoidable time suckers, digital time is often self-inflicted. Statistics prove that the average person checks their phone an average of fifty-eight times a day. While some screen time might be unavoidable due to work and family responsibilities, doomscrolling and mindless online activities can not only take away time you could use for self-care but can also add stress to your life.

It might seem that you’re relaxing while scrolling in line at the post office, but the constant input can actually drain your brain even more. People often scroll because their brains are desperately seeking an easy escape, but digital input is still input. Because of this, it doesn’t actually let your brain relax.

Reduce your screen time by deleting any unnecessary apps. By reducing the clutter, not only will you be more efficient when you do use it, but you will also eliminate the temptation to play one more game or scroll for five more minutes.

Instead, use your phone to connect with friends, not just their profiles. Or use your phone to be more efficient at the things you need to do, so you can make time for the things you want to do. Calendar apps can help keep you organized and intentional with your time.

Replace the habit of scrolling with something healthier. Use waiting time to take deep breaths or to observe the world around you instead. This will give your brain and emotions a much-needed break more than scrolling ever could.

Engage with the Prince of Peace

As a Christian, you have a powerful stress-reduction superweapon at your disposal. Christ is known in the Bible as the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). God knows your busy schedule, the importance of that meeting, and your worry about not spending enough quality time with your children. And He wants to help.

The Bible is full of encouraging and wise verses that address stress directly. Matthew 11:28, for instance, tells you that your burdens can be given to God and in return, He will grant you peace. Psalm 46:10, 1 Peter 5:7, and a host of other Scriptures offer you simple reminders to be still and remember that you belong to God or to cast your anxieties on Him.

When you’re feeling overwhelmed by your day, take a moment to read these encouraging verses. Or better yet, memorize them so you can tuck them away in your heart and recall them at a moment’s notice.

A quick prayer is also an effective way to help reduce feelings of being overwhelmed. Not only does it give you the opportunity to acknowledge your stress and put words to the emotions, but it also invites the Prince of Peace Himself into your day. Listening to and singing worship songs can also help to set your mind on God rather than feeling overwhelmed.

Outside Help and Self-Care for Burnout

If, after you reclaim your time and practice micro moments of self-care, you’re still feeling overwhelmed, it’s wise to seek outside support. A professional mental health specialist can help you learn to be efficient so that you can maximize your self-care time. They can help you identify and confront intrusive thoughts, help you manage your relationships, and most importantly, they can point you to the loving and peaceful arms of your Heavenly Father.

Call one of the therapists at this office and make an appointment to finally make a plan for overcoming self-care for burnout.

item.title: What is EMDR Therapy? Is it the Right Course of Treatment for You?
item.description:
You may have heard of the term EMDR. Lately, EMDR has grown in popularity as an effective mental health treatment to resolve deeper wounds, memories, and/or experiences from your past. Simply put, Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) is known for its unique holistic body and mind approach that aims to help you process trauma.

Continuing to evolve within psychology and mental health, EMDR is acknowledged as an evidence-based practice designed to alleviate distress using a bilateral stimulation method.

What makes EMDR different from traditional therapy is that EMDR involves less talking. In fact, by following the guidance of the bilateral stimulation of the back-and-forth, side-to-side alternation, your body and brain are healing naturally on their own from this motion, making reactions less intense.

By focusing on this method, you are processing the way your mind and body want you to at your own pace. Talk therapy asks you to reiterate the details of your trauma to your therapist.

Although it may make sense that you would need to know what happened in order to help, resharing every detail of the trauma can often be retraumatizing simply by recounting the story. Your mind and body will inadvertently react as if the danger from the trauma is happening all over again.

What is EMDR? A look back to where it all began

EMDR was developed by psychologist Dr. Francine Shapiro in 1987. She realized while walking in the park that her rapid eye movements from one point to another decreased the negative emotion associated with her distressing memories. The intensity of her thoughts and emotions lessened.

This led her to do her own research through case studies to evaluate the effectiveness of this treatment approach. Shapiro developed her model and approach to EMDR treatment, and within a few years of controlled studies and investigation of the treatment of PTSD, EMDR was found to have “significant decreases in ratings of subjective distress and significant increases in rating of confidence in a positive belief.”

In 1990, Shapiro conducted her first EMDR training for licensed mental health professionals. Since then, there have been hundreds of case studies that have shown the effectiveness of cognitive changes, and it is recognized as an effective PTSD treatment.

Though EMDR has been surrounded by controversy as a newer approach to psychotherapy that was established and taught through experimental procedures, EMDR and Shapiro have been recognized for providing relief from negative-shaped thoughts, beliefs, emotions, and images stored from unprocessed memories.

Shortly thereafter, the EMDR Institute was created, now known as EMDRIA (EMDR International Association), and has since held conferences and trainings across the world.

So how does EMDR work?

EMDR follows an Adaptive Information Processing (AIP) model that accesses and processes the traumatic memories or experiences you have had. This model looks at how your brain stores traumatic memories from your past differently than a more normal memory. When a disturbing or distressing event occurs, your brain doesn’t store memories smoothly.

There is a disconnection between what you experienced and what your brain remembers. Because your brain remembers the experience a certain way and hasn’t healed or processed it, your brain doesn’t understand that the danger it felt from it is over. Your brain and body are sensitive to the danger, pain, and injury it experienced from the memory, whether remembered or suppressed.

By looking at your past, present, and future, EMDR therapy addresses your full lifespan, knowing that by processing your past, it will provide you with the ability to be less activated by a present trigger that’s connected to your past. EMDR aims to relieve you of your distress, shift negative beliefs, and help you move past the things that caused you to be stuck.

What does EMDR therapy involve?

EMDR consists of eight phases that occur over multiple therapy sessions. The exact length of EMDR treatment varies person to person based on their needs and how the processing of the eight phases goes.

Typically, most people do a standard 55-minute therapy session once a week, taking time between therapy sessions to give their brain and body rest. However, some prefer doing a lot of work in a shorter amount of time in an EMDR therapy intensive (full-day, multi-day therapy session).

The Eight Phases

History and Information Gathering

This phase begins with an intake, gathering information about your past and what brings you to therapy. Additional information gathering may include checking for your level of dissociation, substance abuse, any suicide or self-harm risk, and medical issues that could impact your EMDR reprocessing.

Your therapist will see if EMDR treatment is a fit for what your goals are, assess your readiness, and will develop a treatment plan for the selected traumatic events you’ve shared.

Preparation

Your therapist will explain any necessary EMDR information, terms, and what you can expect. Your internal and external resources will be assessed and strengthened to prepare for coping with and handling any emotional disturbance that comes up during and in between therapy sessions. The next four phases (3-6) often happen together to reprocess an event or memory.

Assessment

The assessment phase looks deeper into an image, negative belief, emotions, and body sensations, and is measured using the Subjective Unit of Disturbance (SUD) scale and the Validity of Cognition (VOC) scale.

Desensitization

Desensitization occurs while focusing on the traumatic event while simultaneously engaging in side-to-side Bilateral Stimulation (BLS) through eye movements, sounds, taps, or buzzers. This continues until your SUD number reduces to zero. During this phase, new thoughts, sensations, images, and feelings may arise, which is part of the desensitization and reprocessing of the memory.

Installation

When desensitization is done, installation begins, where you strengthen a positive belief with the memory you were processing.

Body Scan

In this phase, you are asked to imagine the memory or event in your mind with the negative belief shared during the assessment phase. Then you are to scan your full body to see if any lingering body sensations are still present.

Closure and Stabilization

In every session that entails phases 3-6, your therapist will end it with phase 7 closure. With guidance from your therapist, you will return to a state of calmness and bring your awareness back to the present, whether you have completed the reprocessing of the memory or not. This allows you to be clear of any disturbances in your mind and body so you can go back to your typical day-to-day life.

Reevaluation and Continuing Care

At the beginning of each therapy session, you and your therapist will briefly check in and discuss your last processed memory and where the distress level is with it. If there appears to be residual distress, you may need to go back to phases 3-7 of the same memory. But if the distress remains low and the positive belief is strong, you may proceed to a new memory and continue your treatment plan and/or process future events related to the memory worked on.

Is EMDR the right course of treatment for you?

EMDR emphasizes that your distressing memory will not go away, as we cannot erase our past. But what EMDR helps do is shift the way your brain recalls it from something that once felt distressing or in control of you into a memory that knows that the event occurred, it does not impact you, and it is something that occurred as part of your story.

EMDR calms your nervous system, brings you from survival mode to thriving, and gives your brain the message that you are not in danger anymore. When you have something that triggers you in your present, and the trigger feels similar to the memory you processed, your reaction will be minimal and less negatively impactful due to the time you took to process and reshape the way your brain and body remembers it.

After reading all of this and you still are not sure if EMDR is the right type of therapy treatment for you, contact us and talk to an EMDR therapist who can answer your questions directly. I provide EMDR to both adult individuals and couples seeking relief from areas where they feel stuck.

item.title: Mental Health Crisis: How to Know You’re in One, and What to Do
item.description:
Life can hit hard at times. Despite our best laid plans and our most cherished hopes, we can find ourselves discouraged by life in ways we may never have expected. What do you do, for instance, when you find yourself in a mental health crisis?

Some say that health is everything, and your mental health certainly affects how you experience the world and the ways you contribute to it. Experiencing a crisis can be a significant roadblock. Just as you need to pay attention to your physical health, you also need to keep tabs on your mental health.

What Is a Mental Health Crisis?

The word ‘crisis’ might convey a situation where everything is falling apart in a rather dramatic fashion. If this is how you understand or experience a crisis, that can potentially stand in the way of you taking the necessary steps to look after yourself. A crisis can be when things simply seem overwhelming, and that includes those moments and seasons of quiet desperation that could be easy to miss.

We all have our hard days, and we sometimes have entire seasons of hardship and stress. Talking about a mental health crisis isn’t referring to this. Rather, when a person is experiencing a crisis, they are at the point where their psychological or emotional pain has become overwhelming. They struggle to care for themselves, function properly, or make safe decisions that promote their wellbeing and that of others around them.

A mental health crisis doesn’t necessarily happen all at once in a dramatic fashion. Sometimes it does, in the wake of experiences such as loss, trauma, or prolonged suffering. At other times, the crisis happens on the back of long seasons of struggle, building up slowly until the weight becomes too difficult to bear.

Believers are not immune to such challenges, as we find story after story in Scripture where individuals are deeply distressed and crying out to the Lord in anguish. Think of Elijah and what might be described as spiritual burnout and suicidal despair after his contest with the prophets of Baal. Collapsed under a broom tree, he begs the Lord to take his life (1 Kings 19:1-18).

There are other examples, like Job’s deep despair and grief after his severe losses, when he no longer sees meaning in his life. He curses the day of his birth (Job 3:1). Or Hannah, whose longing for a child and the mockery from her husband’s other wife led her into deep distress and bitter weeping. We read that she didn’t eat and, “In her deep anguish Hannah prayed to the Lord, weeping bitterly” (1 Samuel 1:10, NIV).

These moments of crisis come to all of us at one point or another. They can be overwhelming to the point where we despair of life itself, but they are not signs that the Lord has abandoned us. The Lord meets us in those spaces of darkness, comforting us (2 Corinthians 1:3-7, NIV). It’s important to be able to recognize those moments of a mental health crisis so that we can receive the necessary help and support.

Signs of a Mental Health Crisis

Pinpointing when you’re going through a mental health crisis can make a huge difference. If you know what’s going on and you take early steps at intervention, you can start moving toward better health and wellbeing, preventing the situation from deteriorating further. If you want to know if you or a loved one is in a mental health crisis, some of the signs to look out for include:

  • Inability to cope: This might look like feeling overwhelmed and unable to manage day-to-day decisions or tasks.
  • Overwhelming sense of hopelessness: A persistent and deep belief or feeling that your situation will never improve and that life is not worth living could be a sign of a mental health crisis. This might also manifest as a person saying that others would be “better off without them.” This is a signal that someone is undergoing crisis, and it shouldn’t be dismissed as a passing thought.
  • Inability to sleep or eat: A severe disruption to basic functioning, such as sleeping or eating, over several days, could point to a person being in crisis.
  • Disconnection from reality: If a person is seeing or hearing things that others around them cannot, or they feel like the world around them is not real, that may also point to a mental health crisis.
  • Reckless or dangerous behavior: Making risky decisions, starting or increasing substance use, or engaging in behaviors that seem self-destructive, like unprotected sex with multiple partners, gambling, or reckless driving, are all signs to take note of.
  • Intrusive or racing thoughts: Another sign to look out for is thoughts that are impossible to quiet or having thoughts that are frightening to you or feel out of control. These thoughts may pop up at random moments, and they cause significant distress.
  • Extreme withdrawal: We all need moments and space to ourselves, but when a person drastically reduces their interactions with friends, family, their church community, or they steer clear of activities that brought them joy or meaning, that could signal a mental health crisis.
  • Giving away possessions: A person giving away the things they own and reasonably need for everyday life could be a sign that a person is in crisis and preparing to end their life.
  • Talk or thoughts of suicide or self-harm: When a person thinks about, expresses a desire to, or attempts to harm themselves or end their own life, that indicates they are in crisis. This must be taken seriously, and steps should be taken immediately to seek the appropriate help, whether by dialing 911 or a crisis hotline.

Dealing with a Mental Health Crisis

What should you do if you or a loved one is experiencing a mental health crisis? Depending on the situation, you can take steps that help to stabilize the crisis and start to move the needle toward safety and healing. For instance, if there is a risk of harm or suicide, call for help immediately, whether that’s 911 or a suicide and crisis lifeline. Don’t hesitate to take active steps to seek help.

If there is a risk of self-harm, it’s important that you safely secure or remove dangerous items such as weapons, medications, or other items that can be used in this manner. Call on someone who can help with this.

Other steps that you can take would include not seeking isolation but instead reaching out to a trusted person. That could be your pastor, a wise friend, or a family member who can be physically with you and work through the crisis. When in crisis, it’s often tempting and easier to simply retreat into yourself. This only serves to deepen despair. It’s important to connect and stay connected, even though that may feel uncomfortable.

If you already have and are working with a psychiatrist or therapist, you can also reach out to them directly so that they can walk with you through the crisis. Many practices have their protocols for dealing with established clients in crisis.

Accept help from your mental health provider and allow others to care for you. Opening up space for others to care for you isn’t a sign of weakness or faithlessness. It’s wisdom that recognizes that we need each other, and that’s how the body of Christ functions (Romans 12:15-16).

You can also take time to ground yourself in the present, whether that’s through breathing slowly, placing your feet flat on the floor or on the grass, or naming five things you can see. In the moment, this can disrupt panic or anxiety, giving you room to seek help. Do this instead of using substances like alcohol or drugs to cope, as these only serve to impair your judgment and increase the risk of making damaging decisions.

As you experience the crisis, don’t minimize what you’re feeling or tell yourself to just push on without seeking help, especially if you’re having suicidal thoughts. Pray and invite the Lord into the season or moment, but reach out for help from others. The Lord uses community, doctors, and counselors as instruments of healing, and wisdom means making use of these gifts.

Lastly, don’t make major life decisions during a crisis, and don’t carry this struggle alone. You must wait until you’re stable and supported before you make major decisions like quitting your job, ending a marriage, moving house, or making other kinds of irreversible choices. You don’t have to go it alone. The journey of long-term healing will take time, and you need others along the way.

Your path toward healing and wholeness might include a combination of professional therapy, medication, and lifestyle changes to help support your wellbeing. Your counselor can walk with you through every stage of that journey. You can contact our reception team to schedule an appointment and begin that journey today.

item.title: What Are Signs of Bipolar Disorder in Women?
item.description:
The signs of bipolar disorder in women can mimic other conditions or worsen due to stress and hormonal changes. Intense episodes of manic and depressive states can shift quickly, leaving problems in relationships, physical health, work, school, sleep, appetite, and judgment.

Once you know the signs of bipolar disorder in women, you can begin to look for patterns and seek professional help.

Signs of Bipolar Disorder in Women

The signs of bipolar disorder in women can only be diagnosed by a medical professional after assessing symptom persistence, severity, and patterns. You may experience manic episodes that can last from seven days to several months, while depressive episodes can range from 14 days to 6 months or more.

Manic Symptoms

Manic symptoms appear as over-the-top behavior. During a manic episode, the woman may flit from one thing to another, take on more responsibilities than is realistic, and seem uncharacteristically loud and talkative. Manic episodes are just one-half of bipolar disorder in women, followed closely by depressive episodes.

Rapid Movements and Speech

Manic behavior includes rapid movements and speech. The woman with bipolar disorder may move quickly or have jerky movements. She speaks rapidly and loudly, making it hard to interrupt or talk over her. People may need to tell her to slow down or ask her to repeat herself.

Racing Thoughts

Thoughts come at a rapid-fire pace. She may try to tackle too many tasks at once, flitting about from idea to idea. She may leave tasks half-done or stop mid-sentence because a new thought occurred to her. People may struggle to follow her line of thought.

Little Sleep

A woman with bipolar disorder may be able to get away with only three to four hours of sleep per night and feel rested during the day. She may stay up late cleaning house or working on projects, sleep a few hours, then go straight into work.

Grandiose Thinking

Bipolar manic episodes can lead a woman to believe she is invincible and more important than she is at work, in relationships, and to the world at large. She may adopt grandiose thinking and believe she is entitled to certain benefits.

Easily Distracted

As the mind races, the woman with bipolar disorder may struggle to stay focused. She may become easily distracted by others, sounds, and smells. She may interrupt herself to comment on a distraction and lose her train of thought. Others may find this aggravating, especially at work when projects don’t get done, or deadlines aren’t met.

Impulsive Actions

Manic episodes can make people lean towards impulsive actions and rash decisions. They may end relationships, quit jobs, or walk out of conversations. This is also a time when a woman struggling with bipolar disorder may say things she doesn’t mean.

Poor Judgment, Especially with Money

Manic episodes can lead to poor judgment, especially with money. The woman may spend as if there’s no limit, letting bank accounts go into the negative or applying for more credit cards. She may make impulse purchases or buy things to show off.

Depressive Symptoms

Depressive symptoms in bipolar disorder in women can vary, but most notably include persistent sadness that can last for weeks or months. Bipolar depression can last longer if left untreated.

Persistent Sadness

Persistent sadness is the hallmark symptom of depression. This sadness can include feelings of emptiness, numbness, and a nonchalant attitude towards people and situations.

Fatigue and Low Energy

There is a bone-deep weariness that sets in with depression. The woman in a depressive state may feel tired all the time, even after sleeping well during the night. Small tasks may seem like too much effort, such as bathing, grooming, and making meals.

Loss of Interest in Hobbies, Socializing, and Other Things That Brought Pleasure

The woman with depression can lose interest in the things that always brought her pleasure. Hobbies, social events, and even television shows can fall by the wayside.

Rapid Appetite and Weight Changes

Depression can bring about rapid appetite and weight changes. She may not feel like eating due to hunger hormone imbalances, or she may emotionally eat to make herself feel better. Noticeable weight gain or loss can occur during this time.

Trouble Concentrating

Depression can make it difficult to focus on work or other tasks. Brain fog and forgetfulness are common. This can cause problems at work and jeopardize a woman’s job.

Suicide Ideation

Depression can feel like it’s never-ending. This can bring about negative thoughts of self-harm and death. If you are struggling with depression and suicidal thoughts, seek help immediately.

Local Treatment for Bipolar Disorder in Women

Treatment is available for the signs of bipolar disorder in women. You can find our Christian counseling center in your local area for in-person sessions, or you can choose virtual sessions from the comfort of your own home. Since the signs of bipolar disorder in women can mirror other conditions, seek professional help from one of the counselors in our association to overcome the symptoms and break the cycle.

item.title: Finding It Hard to Rebuild Routines After Loss? A Good Grief Therapist Can Help
item.description:
Many people grow up believing that staying quiet about pain keeps life calm. Sadness, anger, and grief get easily pushed aside so that daily duties keep moving.

After a loss, that kind of habit or coping mechanism usually stops working. Grief has a way of staying present, even when no one speaks about it. It can sit in the background and affect your focus, sleep, and energy. Simple habits that once felt normal, such as making breakfast, answering messages, or stepping out for errands, may suddenly feel confusing or empty.

After losing someone close, daily life no longer follows the same rhythm. The person who shared those routines is gone, and the silence feels more pronounced than expected. Rebuilding routines after loss does not mean leaving your loved one behind. It means learning how to live in a changed world while keeping their memory close.

What you might need is a therapist for grief who offers guidance that goes beyond comfort and gives you structure, patience, and steady support while daily life slowly takes shape again.

Why Routines Feel so Difficult After Loss

Loss affects more than emotions. It affects the body, the mind, and daily habits. Grief uses energy, even on quiet days. Tasks that once felt easy now demand more effort.

  • Emotional tiredness plays a large role. Grief pulls attention inward, leaving less focus for chores, work, or conversations.
  • Motivation also fades. Without the presence of a loved one, many routines feel pointless.
  • Meals lose flavor. Weekends feel long, and planning feels strange.
  • Daily tasks also carry reminders. Cooking a familiar meal or driving a certain route brings back memories that hurt. These reminders appear without warning and interrupt the day.
  • Many people pull back from social routines as well. Work meetings, family gatherings, and casual plans feel draining.

None of this reflects weakness. These reactions reflect loss. Naming these changes helps reduce shame and opens the door to healing.

The Role of Modern Life in Grief

Grief does not pause while life keeps moving. Messages still arrive, work continues, and responsibilities wait. Many people feel pressure to return to normal quickly, even when grief remains close.

Social media adds another layer. Photos, memories, and posts appear without warning and stir emotions. Work expectations push productivity, even when focus feels low. Family duties continue, especially for parents or caregivers who carry grief while caring for others.

Digital communication also drains energy. Responding to texts or calls feels demanding when emotions run deep. A therapist for grief helps set boundaries during this time. Therapy supports clear communication, self-kindness, and realistic expectations while life continues to move forward.

Everyday Routines That Change After Loss

Grief reaches into every part of daily life. Some routines feel harder than others, especially those once shared with a loved one.

  • Mornings feel different. Waking up, making coffee, or starting the day alone brings quiet that feels sharp.
  • Work routines also suffer. Focus slips, deadlines feel distant, and energy drops.
  • Social routines change as well. Answering messages, attending events, or sitting in groups feels tiring.
  • Health habits receive less care. Eating balanced meals, moving the body, or attending appointments feels like too much effort.
  • Household tasks also bring stress. Cleaning, cooking, or managing bills once shared now rest on one set of shoulders.

A therapist for grief helps reframe these routines. Instead of seeing them as reminders of loss, routines slowly become ways to care for yourself while honoring the past.

Rebuilding Your Routines with Meaning

Healing grows stronger when routines hold meaning. Instead of forcing old habits to return, therapy supports the creation of routines that reflect the present reality.

  • Memory rituals bring comfort. Lighting a candle, writing in a journal, or listening to meaningful music keeps the connection alive.
  • Gentle health habits also help. Short walks, simple meals, and quiet breaks support both body and mind.
  • Connection routines matter as well. Scheduling time with trusted friends or family adds support without pressure.
  • Creative outlets provide another path. Writing, drawing, or music offers release when words feel hard to speak.
  • Rest also receives respect. Quiet reflection, prayer, or meditation helps restore energy.

These routines support life alongside grief. They allow space for sadness while encouraging steady care.

Why Professional Support Matters

Support from friends and family offers comfort, yet professional care provides something different. A therapist for grief brings training, experience, and structure during a time filled with uncertainty.

Therapy offers a safe place for honest expression. Feelings receive space without judgment or advice. Sessions bring consistency when life feels scattered. Therapists tailor support to each person’s needs rather than offering general comfort.

Professional guidance also supports long-term growth. Therapy focuses on living well while grief remains part of the story. The goal involves building strength, understanding patterns, and creating routines that support health and meaning.

How a Therapist for Grief Supports You

Having the support of a grief therapist does not take away pain. Therapy is meant to help people carry grief in a healthier way while daily life slowly returns. Sessions offer guidance, structure, and understanding during a time that feels uncertain.

Their role is:

Breaking routines into small steps: Instead of tackling everything at once, a therapist helps you focus on manageable actions. They provide tools, perspective, and emotional support so you can slowly reintroduce structure into your life.

Validating your experience: They remind you that struggling with routines is not laziness, it’s pain.

Teaching coping strategies: From mindfulness to journaling, therapists offer practical tools to handle emotional triggers.

Encouraging balance: They help you rebuild routines that include rest, connection, and self-care.

Providing accountability: Regular sessions give you a safe space to reflect on progress and setbacks.

Well-rounded therapy connects directly to daily life. Guidance stays practical and realistic.

For morning struggles, a therapist may suggest one small action. Opening the curtains, washing your face, or drinking warm tea builds momentum. For work challenges, therapy supports honest communication with employers about temporary changes or flexible schedules.

Social withdrawal is another area that should receive meaningful attention. Attending a gathering for a short time and leaving early protects energy while maintaining connection. Health habits should be paid equal attention to. Trying new meals that hold fewer memories reduces emotional strain. These small actions add up over time and rebuild routines at a steady pace.

Grief also affects sleep patterns and decision-making. Rest may feel uneven, while choices feel harder than before. A therapist during this time helps identify healthy sleep habits and supports clearer thinking, allowing daily responsibilities to feel more manageable over time without pressure.

Honoring Your Loved One While Moving Forward

Rebuilding routines does not erase memories. Many people choose to honor loved ones through simple practices woven into daily life.

Cooking a favorite dish once a week keeps traditions alive. Placing a photo nearby during quiet reflection offers comfort. Volunteering or donating to causes that mattered to them brings purpose. Writing letters when emotions feel strong allows expression without pressure.

These practices keep the connection present while daily life continues to grow.

Rebuilding routines after loss takes patience and care. Grief changes daily life in ways that feel confusing and tiring. A therapist for grief offers guidance during this process, helping daily habits return with care and meaning.

A therapist for grief helps you take small, meaningful steps toward healing, offering guidance when daily life feels heavy. If you’re finding it hard to rebuild routines after loss, don’t carry the weight alone.

Call the numbers on the screen or book a session today to talk to someone who can help put things back into perspective. With the right support, you can begin to live in a healthy way again, just as your late loved one would have wanted you to.

item.title: Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication
item.description:
For years, she thought she was simply “too sensitive.” Crowded stores felt exhausting. Bright lights were distracting. Conversations in groups felt overwhelming, and she often replayed them in her mind afterward, wondering if she had said the wrong thing. Many women spend years believing they are shy, anxious, or “too much,” only to discover later in life that Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may help explain experiences they have had since childhood.

Autism in women is often diagnosed at a much later age because the signs are either missed or diagnosed under different ailments (1). But when a woman does receive a diagnosis of ASD, there is promising research for treatments that do not rely as heavily on medication.

What Is Autism Spectrum Disorder?

ASD is a developmental, neurodivergent condition that involves significant challenges in communication and social interaction, as well as limitations in behavior patterns. This includes repetitive, highly limited or restricted interests, and inflexibility, among others. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria were updated by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022.

If you think you or a loved one may have ASD but have yet to be diagnosed, we recommend seeing a licensed therapist in one of our offices to discuss your concerns.

Why Autism in Women Gets Missed

There are several reasons a girl may be categorized as “normal” or as having a shy personality or possibly diagnosed with anxiety instead of autism when she’s growing up.

One reason is that anyone — female or male — who is naturally less expressive will not exhibit the expressive signs of another more overt personality who is struggling with social interaction. Another reason is that some of the research used to set the gold standard of autism measures was set using boys as the model, and girls present differently (1).

While a boy with autism may be flagged for an evaluation because he limits his toys to dinosaurs and stacks them repeatedly, a girl may not be flagged because she is playing with her dolls. However, what a teacher or parent might not notice is that within her pretend play, the girl is also exhibiting behavioral patterns that would signify the need for further assessment.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

References

2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735
  • Narayan, A. J., Lieberman, A. F., & Masten, A. S. (2021). Intergenerational transmission and prevention of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Clinical Psychology Review, 85, 101997.

item.title: It Is Not Too Late: Parental Regret and Reconciliation
item.description:
Many parents experience moments of regret in their relationships with their children. It could be a harsh word spoken in anger, years of emotional distance that was never addressed, or a relationship with a child that slowly drifted into something unrecognizable. These are the kinds of things that stay. Regret over these moments is a weight that doesn’t fade, and for many parents, it quietly shapes every interaction that comes after.

Many adult children carry wounds that become part of how they move through the world. It’s hard to address parental regret and the hope of reconciliation in a single conversation or a grand gesture. It is a process, layered and complicated by grief, pride, and hidden pain.

Both parents and adult children need to move toward healing with intention. That kind of intentionality is harder than it sounds when the wounds run deep, and the history between them is long and complicated. Still, we can rest on the promise in Scripture: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NIV)

Understanding the Weight of Parental Regret

Parental regret extends beyond wishing things had gone differently. It carries a particular kind of anguish with the knowledge that the people most affected were children who had no choice in the matter. That weight often shows up as a sense of helplessness, as though a parent feels trapped in an identity they can’t escape. And for many, that feeling doesn’t go away on its own.

This is similar to moral injury, which occurs when emotional damage stems from the gap between who a person wanted to be and who they actually were. That type of shame lingers long after the moment has passed. Most parents manage it privately rather than address it directly. That isolation only deepens the wound over time.

Parental regret is especially complex because of its intersection with love. Loving someone and knowing you caused them harm produces a grief that is hard to name. It shows up as depression, as anger turned inward, or as a quiet belief that repair is no longer possible.

Parents in these situations find themselves maneuvering between the desire to reach out and the fear that doing so will only cause more damage. That leaves the relationship stuck in a painful place, where both individuals carry wounds that were never named out loud. But God knows, and we can invite Him into our pain. “Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts.” (Psalm 139:23, NIV)

The Emotional Landscape of Adult Children in Parental Regret and Reconciliation

The decision to address parental regret and reconciliation is not simple for adult children. It involves navigating painful memories, weighing the emotional cost of restoration, and sitting with feelings that don’t have easy answers. Adult children often grieve for the parent they needed and the relationship they never had. Both of those things are true at the same time. Both deserve space rather than a rush to resolution.

Reconciliation doesn’t automatically restore what was broken. It requires trust, and trust takes time to rebuild. The idea of opening the door again often feels like a risk for adult children who have tried before without anything changing.

There is also a quiet social pressure to forgive quickly or to minimize what happened to preserve family harmony. That pressure produces reconciliation that looks good but is far from the real thing. When an adult child goes through the motions without genuine safety or acknowledgment, it can deepen the wound rather than begin to close it.

Christian counselors emphasize that there is no way to manufacture or hurry genuine reconciliation. It is only reached through an intentional choice free from manipulation or guilt, and grounded in honesty about what happened. Scripture helps us in this: “Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.” (Colossians 3:13, NIV) This shows us how to handle these hard situations.

What Makes Parental Regret and Reconciliation Possible

The reconciliation that happens between a parent and a child does not come from both parties pretending the past didn’t occur. It only takes shape when both people are willing to face it honestly, with genuine acknowledgment of harm, rather than an apology offered to relieve personal guilt. Accountability forms the foundation of repair. It only holds when someone chooses to face what they did without deflecting.

When a parent takes responsibility without minimizing, without deflecting, and without asking the adult child to move faster than they are ready, it gives the adult child permission to be exactly where they are. That can feel vulnerable for the parent who doesn’t know how that honesty will land.

Faith plays a significant role in this process for families. Biblically, there is a call toward reconciliation rooted in truth and grace, not a mandate to ignore boundaries or overlook pain. Christian counselors help families understand that forgiveness and reconciliation are related but not the same.

Forgiveness can begin in the heart long before reconciliation is possible. Sometimes reconciliation has to wait until safety is established. When both take root, the result is a relationship that is more honest and grounded than what existed before. Jesus put a high value on reconciliation.

“Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift.” – Matthew 5:23-24, NIV

Mental Health, Faith, and the Journey Toward Healing

Repairing a parent-child relationship has a deep impact on mental health that is hard to keep hidden. The emotional work involved isn’t always easy to see from the outside. Depression, anxiety, and difficulty forming attachments in adulthood connect back to unresolved relational wounds. This is particularly true when those wounds go all the way back to the earliest relationships a person ever had.

The way parents connect with children at a young age is a big influence on the ability of the child to develop emotional regulation and experience intimacy throughout their lives. Because of this, the stakes of parental regret and reconciliation extend beyond the family unit. Moving toward reconciliation isn’t just about repairing one relationship. Reconciliation focuses on reclaiming and healing something that was hurt long ago.

Parents who grapple with regret find that the mental health implications run just as deep. Chronic guilt and shame, when left unaddressed, lead to withdrawal, self-isolation, and a diminished sense of personal worth. Parents carry an internal picture of what a good parent looks like. When they believe they missed that mark, it builds a kind of trap that doesn’t open easily without the support of a therapeutic relationship.

Shame does not have to be the outcome. When parents find their way into a space where their story can be heard without judgment, that cycle can begin to shift. It doesn’t happen overnight. But it does happen.

Christian counselors work at the intersection of faith and clinical support. That combination matters here because this kind of healing rarely happens without both.

Pursuing Healing

Reconciliation does not erase what happened or negate the pain that came from it. It is a painfully slow and tender decision to build something new from the rubble of what fell apart. Everyone involved must show up with honesty, patience, and a willing heart – and stay present even when it gets uncomfortable.

Not every relationship heals completely. That does not mean anyone has failed. It means grace is still needed. For those who take the first steps toward addressing parental regret and reconciliation, the healing potential is real. Scripture teaches us that grace goes beyond what any of us can accomplish alone. Something new can take place even in the middle of the chaos of regret and reconciliation.

And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose. – Romans 8:28, NIV

If you are facing the challenge of reconciliation and carrying a weight of regret, you do not have to navigate it alone. The first step toward something better is reaching out. Contact our reception team to learn more about parental regret and reconciliation and to get connected with a counselor who understands the complexities of family relationships.

item.title: Relationship Depression: 11 Red Flags and How to Cope
item.description:
Relationship depression is a term used to describe depression that develops as a result of a problematic relationship. It is not a formal medical diagnosis.

Often cyclical in nature, it tends to create a loop in which the relationship problems that trigger the depression aggravate the depressed person’s symptoms. This increases the disconnect between them and their partner, creating frustration or resentment. It further damages their relationship dynamics through conflicts caused by a lack of communication and misunderstandings.

Relationships and Mental Health

Studies show that there is a close link between mental health and the quality of your relationships. Strong, supportive relationships, for instance, provide comfort, security, emotional support, and connection. This can give your mood a boost, help you maintain a positive outlook on life, and have a beneficial impact on your overall mental well-being.

Toxic or abusive relationships, on the other hand, can lead you to question your self-worth. They can also cause you to feel stressed, anxious, or depressed. Negative thinking patterns can arise that may contribute to or activate an underlying mental health struggle.

Because of this interconnectedness, any relationship can become strained by the symptoms of depression. It begins as the depressed person starts to withdraw from his or her partner and seems to lose interest in the things they used to enjoy doing together. Communication deteriorates, which can be misinterpreted as rejection and falling out of love. The depression is causing him or her to struggle to connect and making even simple interactions feel exhausting.

Possible Causes of Relationship Depression

There is no one definitive cause of relationship depression, but contributing factors can include a range of issues. Some possible examples include:

  • A spouse’s infidelity
  • Having your trust betrayed by your spouse
  • Physical or emotional abuse
  • Being consistently disappointed by the person you thought you could rely on
  • Communication breakdowns that cause you to feel misunderstood or emotionally disconnected
  • Unresolved conflicts that keep piling up
  • Financial stress
  • Mismatched expectations about roles and responsibilities in the relationship

Common Red Flags of Relationship Depression

Relationship depression tends to sink in gradually over time, and you may not notice the subtle changes in your thoughts and behavior patterns. If left unrecognized and unaddressed, however, it can impact every area of your life. It can interfere with your ability to interact with others in a healthy way and even impair your capacity to engage in your day-to-day responsibilities.

Common red flags that should not be ignored include:

Persistent sadness You may experience persistent sadness and frequent tears without knowing why.

Negative outlook You may feel helpless and hopeless, unable to see anything in a positive light, believe life isn’t worth living, and/or have thoughts of death or suicide.

Low self-esteem You may believe that you are a failure, worthless, unlovable, or a burden, and therefore pull away from the other person rather than express your needs or ask for help.

Emotional withdrawal You withdraw from the other person, stop sharing your thoughts and feelings with him or her, avoid eye contact, and are less responsive to his or her needs.

Irritability You may experience mood swings and increased irritability, becoming easily annoyed or frustrated, and snapping at seemingly small things.

Loss of intimacy You experience reduced feelings of affection toward your partner, a decline in physical intimacy, and avoidance of sexual contact.

Physical symptoms You may feel physically or mentally exhausted; experience changes in your sleeping and eating patterns, such as trouble sleeping or sleeping more than usual, or loss of appetite or binge eating; gastrointestinal problems; loss of sexual desire; and unexplained aches or pains.

Impaired communication You have trouble thinking clearly, struggle to articulate your feelings, feel disconnected from the other person, are reluctant to discuss important issues, and your relationship is full of conflict, misunderstandings, and arguments.

Dulling of your emotions You may feel emotionally numb; struggle to connect or express love and affection toward your partner; and feel indifferent to what he or she does or feels.

Loss of interest in things you used to do together Things you and the other person used to enjoy doing together may seem meaningless, and you may find yourself losing interest in doing them.

Distorted perceptions You may, for instance, mistakenly believe your relationship is the cause of your feelings of emptiness and depression, that it has lost its significance, and/or feel trapped or suffocated by it.

Practical Steps to Help You Cope with Relationship Depression

Journal Journaling about your feelings helps you identify and process them, get them out of your head and onto paper, and be able to identify your triggers.

Prioritize self-care Prioritize your health and well-being by getting enough sleep, eating balanced, nutritious meals, staying hydrated, getting some form of regular exercise, and setting healthy boundaries.

Stop listening to the negative Start talking to yourself instead of listening to your negative self-talk. Reject it and replace it with more realistic, positive statements that edify, encourage, and lift you up.

Communicate with your partner Even if you feel too tired to talk, ashamed, or undeserving of anything good, make an effort to have an open, honest conversation with your partner. Talk about your thoughts, feelings, and the symptoms and sensations you are experiencing, so he or she can understand what you are going through. This will help them know how to help and support you.

Avoid isolating Instead of pulling away and isolating, make an effort to connect with your partner, even if it’s just in simple ways such as taking a walk together.

Turn your focus onto God Take your eyes off your present circumstances and focus instead on the truths in God’s Word and on His steadfast, everlasting love for you.

Consider counseling Counseling provides a safe, nonjudgmental space where you can learn to identify and process your feelings and relationship concerns under the guidance of a trained mental health professional. They can also help you determine whether your depression really is being caused by your relationship, or by something else going on in your life.

How To Help and Support a Depressed Partner

Get informed Learning as much as you can about depression and its symptoms can help you better identify and understand what your partner is struggling with, identify the signs, and not take his or her behavior personally.

Talk about it Instead of ignoring the issue, talk to your partner about what you are seeing without being critical or judgmental. Ask what he or she is feeling, and offer encouragement and validation.

Be patient and empathetic Be patient and empathetic toward your partner and offer a listening ear. Let them know that you love and support them, and be a safe place to turn for validation and understanding. Make sure they know you won’t be dismissive of their feelings.

Work together as a team Ask your partner what you can do and what changes you can make to help him or her deal with his or her symptoms. Let them know that you are there for them and suggest working as a team to identify stressors and triggers together, and brainstorm ways they can cope with them when they arise.

Encourage professional help Encourage your partner to pursue counseling, and offer to go with them.

To learn more or address relationship depression in your life, counseling can help. If you would like to set up a risk-free appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors in our online directory, please call the office.
